name: traffic-simulation.de (movsim/traffic-simulation-de) and MovSim (movsim/movsim)
type: simulator (lane-based microscopic browser simulator in JavaScript, plus the related Java desktop/CLI simulator MovSim)
maintainer: Martin Treiber (TU Dresden) for traffic-simulation.de; MovSim copyright Arne Kesting, Martin Treiber, Ralph Germ and Martin Budden, under the movsim GitHub organisation.
first_release: traffic-simulation-de GitHub repository created 2016-09-27 (JavaScript version); MovSim repository created 2011-07-01, described in Treiber and Kesting, IEEE ITS Magazine 2010.
last_activity: traffic-simulation-de: last commit 2026-10-29. MovSim: last commit 2026-09-02 ('upgraded dependencies, cleanups'), with dependabot merges in 2025-12.
licence: GPL-3.0 for both (LICENSE file in traffic-simulation-de; MovSim README: 'licensed under GPL version 3', with commercial use by contacting the copyright holders).
language: traffic-simulation-de: JavaScript (about 2.4 MB of JS including English, German and Spanish copies of each scenario; road.js alone 5,242 lines), HTML5 canvas, CSS. MovSim: Java 8+ with Maven (about 1.16 MB of Java), JAXB XML configuration.
code_availability: Full source on GitHub: https://github.com/movsim/traffic-simulation-de (live at https://traffic-simulation.de) and https://github.com/movsim/movsim .
maintenance_health: traffic-simulation-de: single active developer (Treiber), frequent commits, about 1,058 stars and 157 forks; many forks are student copies and drift. Code is per-scenario copy-and-modify (each scenario has .js, _gui.js, and _ger/_es copies), so fixes do not propagate automatically and many README_* files are working notes, some in German or personal email. MovSim (Java): about 340 stars, 94 forks, mainly maintenance updates (dependency bumps) in recent years; its README still references Travis CI.
scale: Microscopic (time-continuous car-following with ballistic update; MovSim Java also includes cellular automata and coupled-map models).
car_following: JS: ACC model (IDM extension with 'coolness' factor, Treiber and Kesting book ch. 12.5) by default, original IDM selectable by replacing 'new ACC' with 'new IDM'; parameters deliberately set to produce very string-unstable traffic for visual effect (README_tips4scientificUse). Acceleration noise QnoiseAccel (default 0.05 to 0.1 m2/s3) and inter-driver variation driver_varcoeff=0.15 on v0 and T. MovSim Java: IDM, ACC/Enhanced IDM, OVM/Bando, Velocity Difference Model, Gipps, Krauss, Nagel-Schreckenberg CA, Kerner-Klenov-Wolf CA, plus memory and noise driver models.
lane_model: Discrete lanes per road link (fixed lane count per link, numbered from the left, lateral coordinate v positive to the right). Lane changes by MOBIL with speed-dependent bSafe to make changes more aggressive in congestion; mandatory lane changes before lane closures and offramps via setLCMandatory and route-driven bias; lane-changing bans by range; minimum waiting times after active and passive changes. Lane changes are instantaneous in logic with smooth drawing.
lateral_model_type: None (discrete lanes). Lateral position within a lane is not modelled; the separate mixedTraffic project is the 2D variant.
junction_model: Network of directed logical road links connected by road.connect(target, uSource, uTarget, offsetLane, conflicts, maxspeed, targetPrio). Vehicles carry a route (sequence of roadIDs). Without conflicts, a connection acts like a pointwise merge (only target-road vehicles are checked). With conflicts, road.determineConflicts checks vehicles on crossing links that are approaching conflict points; the intersection scenario defines per-OD conflict lists for three rule sets (trafficRuleIndex 0 = priority road, 1 = right-before-left, 2 = traffic lights; left turners keep some conflicts under signals). Gap acceptance design notes (README_intersections) use an obstruction criterion plus a time-to-collision threshold of about 3 s. Ramps use road.mergeDiverge over a parallel section, with a standing virtual obstacle at the merge end. Roundabouts are modelled as a ring link with on-ramps and off-ramps for each arm (4-arm design with OD presets and a toggle between ring priority and right priority; a multi-lane roundabout page exists). Red lights are rows of standing virtual obstacle vehicles, one per lane.
signal_control_modes: Fixed-time: TrafficLightControlEditor.js lets users set relative green duration and phase per light; lights can also be toggled by click and dragged from a depot. No actuated or adaptive control, no learned-control hooks. Ramp-metering game lets a human act as controller. MovSim Java supports traffic lights configured in XML.
flyover_support: Partial. On-ramps, off-ramps, merges, diverges, weaving and lane drops are fully supported. Grade separation is implicit: links only interact where explicitly connected, so two links whose drawings cross do not conflict; overpasses are purely a drawing-order trick ('offramp bridge => draw last' in offramp.js, routing.js), and road.js drawing accepts umin/umax 'useful for bridges'.
grade_separation_handling: No layer or elevation model, no import, no checks or repair. Geometry is hand-coded per scenario as trajectory functions x(u), y(u); conflicts and connections are hand-specified. A bridge is just a link drawn last.
vehicle_types: Car and truck (default), obstacles (user-movable and fixed), virtual traffic-light vehicles, ego vehicle id; ids encode type ranges (1 ego, 10-49 clicked, 50-99 obstacles, 100-149 traffic lights, >=200 normal). onramp_scooters.js adds a scooter class (2.5 x 1.5 m, described as 'kind of tricycles' for a 2023 user request); README_carsAndScooters explains rescaling cars and trucks to emulate scooters. Classes differ by length, width, ACC parameters and truck right-lane preference. No motorcycle, auto-rickshaw or bus class by default.
gridlock_policy: Two ad-hoc hacks, reported only to the browser console: (1) road.connect force-hack: if a vehicle on a closing lane stays below 0.2 m/s for 0.8 s it is moved by force onto the target link ('moved by force to new link'); (2) intersection.js with right-before-left rules periodically calls resolveGridlock() for 1.5 s every 10 s, temporarily giving the main road priority. The source notes that keeping all conflicts under signal control 'will lead to gridlocks', so some conflicts are deliberately dropped. No teleport statistics are exposed to users.
mixed_traffic_support: Weak. Two vehicle classes in lanes; heterogeneity only through length, width and parameters. Smaller vehicles cannot share a lane side by side or filter between lanes.
non_lane_behaviour: None in traffic-simulation.de or MovSim; vehicles always occupy exactly one lane. The author's lane-free work is in the separate MTGermany/mixedTraffic project, which is not integrated into this network code.
per_class_parameters: No published Indian per-class values. Defaults are demo values chosen to produce visible stop-and-go waves; the author recommends using the book's standard parameters for scientific use (README_tips4scientificUse). Scooter scenario dimensions: car 5.0 x 2.2 m, truck 12.5 x 3.0 m, scooter 2.5 x 1.5 m (onramp_scooters.js).
indian_calibration_evidence: None found for traffic-simulation.de or MovSim [uncertain].
calibration_dataset_used: None for Indian traffic. The simulator can generate trajectories and leader-follower pairs for external calibration studies (README_trajData4ExternalUse, README_createLFpairs).
calibration_method: Not applicable to the simulator itself; IDM/ACC parameters come from the authors' textbook and published calibrations on German data [uncertain].
validation_against_field_case: None for India. Scenarios are stylised (ring, on-ramp, roadworks, uphill, roundabout, intersection) with some German road names (BaWue, S71) rather than validated field cases.
network_import: traffic-simulation-de: none; every network is hand-coded JavaScript (trajectory functions and connect calls per scenario). MovSim Java: road network described in OpenDRIVE (.xodr) plus XML project files; no OpenStreetMap converter in the repository [uncertain].
demand_input_formats: JS: inflow sliders (veh/h) at upstream boundaries with a fractional inflow buffer, truck fraction slider, route fractions (for example offramp or roundabout OD presets), density slider on the ring road, and micro initialisation via road.initializeMicro. MovSim Java: XML (.xprj) configuration of sources, routes, vehicle types and traffic composition, with CSV output.
data_access: Not a dataset. JS simulator exports trajectory files (road<n>_time<t>.txt, dt_export default 0.5 s) and virtual detector files via a download button.
runs_in_browser_or_server: traffic-simulation.de runs entirely in the browser (static files, setInterval main loop at 30 fps). MovSim runs as a Java desktop viewer or command-line batch simulator on a server or workstation.
wasm_or_streaming_feasibility: JS engine needs no WASM. MovSim Java would need server-side execution with state streamed to the browser, or a port (no WASM build exists [uncertain]).
api: JS: no formal API; pseudo-classes road, vehicle, models (IDM, ACC, MOBIL), TrafficObjects and stationaryDetector, with heavy use of globals and per-scenario setup code. README explains how to add a new model (CACC skeleton via testNewModel flag). MovSim Java: XML config plus command-line; Java library classes in core.
performance: No published vehicle-count benchmarks [uncertain]. README_3d states that the cost of lane changing, re-routing and decision making is negligible even on smartphones and that 3D graphics would cost a multiple; typical scenarios run hundreds of vehicles at 30 fps with time-lapse up to about 6x or more.
multi_tenancy_model: JS: client-side, one simulation per browser tab, static hosting with near-zero server cost. MovSim Java: process per scenario on a server if offered as a service.
build_complexity: JS: zero build (open the HTML file), but embedding is hard: each scenario is a monolithic script with its own globals and GUI; road.js is a 5,000-line class mixing simulation, network connection and drawing. Lifting road.js, models.js, vehicle.js and TrafficObjects.js into a module is a few hours of refactoring. MovSim Java: Maven build, Java 8+.
scenario_editability: Users can change inflow, truck fraction, speed limits, model parameters (v0, T, s0, a, b, politeness), drag obstacles, traffic lights and speed limits onto roads, edit fixed-time signal plans, choose roundabout OD presets and priority rules, and choose intersection rule type. Road geometry, lane counts and widths are fixed per scenario (some scenarios add or remove a lane). No bus stops, parking or network editing UI.
output_metrics_supported: Virtual stationary detectors (flow, speed), trajectory export, travel-time displays in routing games, speed colour maps; coffeemeter game shows ride comfort. No LOS, PCU, queue-length or conflict metrics. MovSim Java: detectors, spatiotemporal fields, floating-car data, travel times, and fuel consumption.
emissions_support: traffic-simulation.de: none found in the JS sources. MovSim Java: physics-based fuel-consumption and emissions model (not HBEFA).
reuse_mode: Inspiration and architecture reference, and optionally port selected code. The road-link plus connect/conflicts/mergeDiverge design, parallel update order, virtual-vehicle traffic lights and inflow-buffer boundary conditions are directly reusable patterns for a lane-based or hybrid browser engine. Not usable as-is for Indian mixed traffic.
effort_within_72_hours: Forking a scenario and re-skinning it (rename trucks/cars, add a motorbike class with small width) could produce a lane-based demo in about 4 to 6 hours, but it would not show lane-free behaviour. Extracting road.js/models.js into a reusable engine with a user-editable network: about 12 to 20 hours, because every network is hand-coded and conflicts are specified manually per OD. Replacing lanes with a continuous lateral model (MTM) inside road.js is a deep rewrite of neighbour search, lane changing, mergeDiverge and connect, likely beyond 72 hours together with UI and OSM import. Cut: roundabouts, right-before-left rules, routing games, multilingual pages, MovSim Java entirely.
licence_constraint: GPL-3.0 for both. Copying JS code into our web app and distributing it to browsers obliges us to release the client code under GPL-3.0 with source. MovSim commercial use requires contacting the copyright holders. Reimplementing the published IDM/ACC/MOBIL equations ourselves avoids the obligation.
known_limitations: (1) Author: intersection and connection logic 'not yet perfect' (README) and right turns need much anticipation heuristics. (2) Parameters chosen for visible instability, not realism (README_tips4scientificUse). (3) Inter-link update is not fully sequential across dependent links (README: 'presently, is not done'). (4) No network import; all geometry and conflicts hand-coded. (5) Lane-based only; no mixed-traffic or lateral model. (6) README_intersections: a full 12-OD X intersection was judged too complex for the original project's intent. (7) Code duplication across scenario and language copies. (8) MovSim Java is mainly in maintenance mode.
documented_failures: Gridlocks at right-before-left intersections when all four arms have waiting vehicles (solved by periodically forcing main-road priority, resolveGridlock); gridlocks when all conflicts are kept under signal control because secondary-road vehicles always 'fear' waiting main-road vehicles (some conflicts dropped); vehicles stuck on closing lanes (force-moved after 0.8 s); README_speedlimit_bug_2019_12 records a speed-limit bug; README_Gridlock email notes that early lane changes in dense traffic cause self-blocking at roadworks.
validation_approach: Model-level validation in the authors' publications and textbook (IDM, ACC, MOBIL, numerical integration comparison in Treiber and Kanagaraj 2015); simulator correctness shown by reproducing qualitative phenomena (stop-and-go waves, capacity drop, bottleneck effects) and by detector and trajectory exports; no published validation of the browser network logic against field junction data.
takeaway_for_our_build: Copy the architecture, not the code: model the network as directed road links with arc-length coordinate u and lateral coordinate v, link-to-link connect(source, uSource, target, uTarget, laneOffset, conflicts) with routes per vehicle, ramps as parallel merge/diverge zones, signals as full-width standing virtual vehicles, and a strict parallel update order (accelerations, then lateral moves, then merges, then positions, then boundary conditions, then connections). From day one build an explicit, counted and user-visible gridlock breaker (timeout plus forced release), because even Treiber needed hidden console-only hacks; and generate conflict lists automatically from geometry rather than hand-coding them per OD.
